steps.description: Diagnose and resolve the 'prompt processing error' by checking input syntax and clarity, then confirm the intended hypothesis with the user before proceeding with any experimental design.

Design and execute a bootstrap rigidity experiment for small feedforward networks. Define the loss function and constraint set, implement a width scan (N_c) over varying constraint counts (w), train networks, evaluate out-of-sample error (max abs error), and compute N_c(w) as the minimal width achieving ≤1e-3 error on held-out constraints. Ensure all outputs are finite and report the rigidity classification (rigid vs fat) based on the trend.

Diagnose the root cause of the 'prompt processing error' by checking input formatting and system parsing, clarify with the user to ensure a well-formed hypothesis is established before proceeding with any experimental design.

Redesign the numerical experiment to properly define rigidity as sublinear growth of minimal width $N_c(w)$ rather than flatness. (1) Define constraint family as polynomial interpolation of degree $d$ with $w = d+1$ constraints. (2) Train small feedforward networks with varying widths $N$ on $w$ constraints using mean-squared error loss. (3) Determine $N_c(w)$ as minimal width achieving max absolute error $\le 10^{-3}$ on both training and held-out points. (4) Analyze scaling behavior: compare $N_c(w)$ against theoretical bounds $O(w)$ (linear capacity) and $O(\sqrt{w})$ (sublinear rigidity candidate). (5) Implement with fixed random seeds and convergence criteria. Prediction: For polynomial interpolation, $N_c(w)$ will grow at least linearly with $w$ (no rigidity), demonstrating that universal approximation requires width scaling with constraint count for exact interpolation tasks.
